implementation_notes: Kotlin on the JVM has the same answer as Java - no managed prefetch intrinsic - so the lever is layout and typed/primitive arrays. Kotlin's value classes and inline classes give a typed-array feel over JVM primitives without boxing overhead, and data classes of primitives in a List still box unless they are primitive specialisations. For coroutine-based workloads the useful form of the pattern is starting the next computation early (launch a coroutine that warms the next page or the next tree node) so the latency overlaps the current one's compute - a coroutine-level prefetch that needs no CPU hint at all. As in Java, measure with async-profiler; on a managed JVM the win is almost always in the layout or in the coroutine overlap, not in a cache hint.
idiom_name: no managed prefetch; layout (arrays of primitives / value classes) plus coroutine overlap to warm the next unit of work
pitfalls: No managed prefetch intrinsic in Kotlin/JVM; the equivalent is layout or coroutine overlap.
List<Double> boxes every element (unlike double[]), so the 'typed array' locality win is lost - use DoubleArray/FloatArray.
Launching a coroutine per element to prefetch defeats the point (context-switch cost exceeds the latency saved); warm a few ahead, not one per item.
A prefetch coroutine that is cancelled leaves the warming incomplete; on a structured-cancellation scope a cancelled warm silently does nothing.
